title: Spanish Preposition Mistakes English Speakers Make

meta_description: Spanish preposition mistakes: the personal a, depender de, pensar en, soñar con, en vs a, verbs that need no preposition, with fixes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: Depend on, think about, dream of: why English prepositions don’t translate.

body_html:
Spanish preposition mistakes happen because English speakers translate prepositions one by one. But “depend on” is depender de, “think about” is pensar en and “dream of” is soñar con. Some English verbs need a preposition where Spanish needs none (“look for” is just buscar), and Spanish adds one English doesn’t have at all: the personal a. Here are the preposition mistakes I see most often, grouped so they’re easy to fix.

Key takeaways
  • Use the personal a before people as direct objects: Veo a María.
  • Learn verbs with their preposition: depender de, pensar en, soñar con, casarse con.
  • Buscar, esperar, escuchar, mirar, pedir take no preposition.
  • En is for where you are; a is for where you go.
{{toc}}

1. Forgetting the personal a

When the direct object is a specific person (or a pet you treat as one), Spanish puts a before it:

  • Conozco a tu hermano. I know your brother.
  • Llamé a mi madre. I called my mum.
  • Busco a mi perro. I’m looking for my dog.

No a before things (Veo la casa) or after tener (Tengo dos hermanos). The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas explains the personal a in detail.

2. Translating the English preposition

arrive in / atllegar enllegar a
be interested ininteresarse sobreinteresarse por

Examples: Depende de ti. (It depends on you.) / Pienso mucho en ti. (I think about you a lot.) / Anoche soñé contigo. (Last night I dreamed about you.) / Llegamos a Madrid a las diez. (We arrived in Madrid at ten.)

{{image:2}}

3. Adding a preposition Spanish doesn’t need

Several common verbs include the meaning of the English preposition:

  • buscar = to look for: Busco las llaves (not busco para)
  • esperar = to wait for: Espero el autobús
  • escuchar = to listen to: Escucho música
  • mirar = to look at: Mira la foto
  • pedir = to ask for: Pedí un café
  • pagar = to pay for: Pagué la cena

The personal a still appears with people: Espero a Juan. See {{link:pedir-vs-preguntar|pedir vs preguntar}} and {{link:oir-vs-escuchar|oír vs escuchar}} for more.

4. En vs a for places

En describes where you are; a describes where you go:

  • Estoy en casa. I’m at home. / Voy a casa. I’m going home.
  • Trabajo en Madrid. / Me mudo a Madrid.

English “at” and “in” both often become en: en la oficina, en el parque, en la fiesta.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

5. Time expressions

  • Days: el lunes (on Monday), not en lunes.
  • Clock times: a las tres (at three).
  • Parts of the day: por la mañana (in the morning) in Spain, en la mañana in much of Latin America.
  • Months and years: en mayo, en 2026.

6. De for material and purpose

English uses noun + noun; Spanish uses de: una mesa de madera (a wooden table), un vaso de agua (a glass of water), la clase de español (Spanish class), un zumo de naranja (orange juice).

7. Por and para

The biggest preposition pair of all deserves its own guide: {{link:por-vs-para|por vs para}}. In short, para points to purpose and destination, por to cause, exchange and route: Gracias por todo, Es para ti.

Why this happens, from a translator’s desk

When I translate between English and Spanish, prepositions are where literal versions break first. English builds meaning with phrasal verbs (look for, look after, look up), while Spanish usually chooses a different verb instead: buscar, cuidar, consultar. So the fix is rarely “find the right preposition”; it is often “find the right verb”. When you are unsure, look the verb up in a good dictionary and note the preposition it takes in the example sentences, then copy that pattern exactly.

Try it yourself

  1. I’m waiting for my sister. (Espero a mi hermana.)
  2. It depends on the price. (Depende del precio.)
  3. She fell in love with Paris. (Se enamoró de París.)
  4. We’re going to the beach on Saturday. (Vamos a la playa el sábado.)
  5. I’m thinking about you. (Estoy pensando en ti.)

Prepositions are one of several mistake families covered in {{link:spanish-mistakes-english-speakers-make|my guide to Spanish mistakes English speakers make}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Don’t translate prepositions; learn them as part of the verb. Write depender de, pensar en and soñar con in your notes as single units, drop the preposition after buscar and esperar, and remember the personal a before people. That alone removes most preposition mistakes.

faq.q: What is the personal a in Spanish?
faq.a: It is the preposition a placed before a specific person who is the direct object: Veo a María, Llamo a mi madre. It is not used before things or usually after tener.

faq.q: Is it depender de or depender en?
faq.a: Depender de: Depende de ti (It depends on you). Depender en is a common English-influenced mistake.

faq.q: Why don’t you say buscar para in Spanish?
faq.a: Because buscar already means “to look for”. Just say Busco mis llaves.
